title: Sajjan's rest house
hookLine: a man who robbed the travelers who slept in his inn hears Nanak sing and gives it all up

lines: A FRIENDLY INN ON A LONG ROAD.
AT NIGHT, THE HOST ROBBED HIS GUESTS.
cards: Picture a rest stop on a long road. Clean, welcoming, run by a man so pleasant that his name, Sajjan, means friend, or good man. He built a place for Hindu travelers to pray and one for Muslim travelers.
He offered a warm meal and a bed. And at night, tradition says, he robbed his guests, killed some of them, and threw their bodies down a well.

One evening two new travelers arrived: a man with a calm face and his friend with a rebab. Sajjan sized up their clothes and their bearing and guessed they carried something worth taking. He showed them to their room.

teach.b: Sajjan waited for them to fall asleep. But Nanak didn't sleep. He asked Mardana to play, and he sang.
The hymn Sikhs link to this night is in the scripture, in raga Suhi, and it's about bronze.

teach.h: BRONZE SHINES, BUT RUB IT: BLACK.
teach.b: Bronze is bright and shiny, the Guru sings, but rub it and the black comes off on your fingers. Wash it a hundred times and it won't come clean. Then more images: tall buildings, painted and grand, hollow inside.
Cranes in white feathers standing in holy water, looking for fish to kill.
Sajjan stood outside the door and heard himself. The shiny front. The prayer rooms for both faiths.
The well. Tradition says he fell at the Guru's feet, confessed everything, and gave back what he'd stolen.
The inn became a place where travelers were actually safe, often remembered as one of the first places the Guru's followers gathered on the road. Notice what Nanak doesn't do.
He doesn't call the guards or expose Sajjan to the town. He sings, and lets the man find the truth himself.

Look back at the week: the first words after the river, the qazi whose mind wandered off to a young horse, Mardana and the rebab, setting out on the road, Lalo and Bhago, milk and blood, and now Sajjan.
The same pattern every time: an outside that looks one way, an inside that's another, and a Guru who gently shows the difference. Sikhs love this story for its last turn.
If even Sajjan turned, nobody is past turning.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Sajjan as a sakhi about transformation through the Guru's word, and the Suhi hymn linked to it is sung in kirtan; tradition places the inn near Tulamba, in present-day Pakistan.

games.q: you're a traveler, and you've worked out that your friendly host plans to rob you tonight. what do you do?
o: call for the guards in the morning.
games.why: Nanak asked Mardana to play and sang about shining bronze. Sajjan, listening at the door, heard himself and fell at his feet.

practice: Name one thing you'd like to put down: not your worst secret, just a habit, a grudge, or a small shiny front you're tired of carrying. Picture setting it on the floor, the way Sajjan set down his loot.
You don't have to do anything else with it yet; just let your hands be empty for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Sajjan. The innkeeper whose name meant friend, who robbed his guests until he heard Guru Nanak sing of shining bronze and turned.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sajjan, a friend, a good person; the story turns on a name that didn't fit, until it did.

carryVoice: Your line: even sajjan turned. Tomorrow, a stranger wades into the Ganges at sunrise. Five weeks, done.
